name: Identifies how a character is connected to their setting
description: Student can describe how a character in a literary text is suited to or shaped by their setting, using evidence from the text.
exampleOfSuccess: Student explains: In the fairytale the witch lives in a dark forest because witches are mysterious and scary — the dark forest matches that. She wouldn't belong in a sunny garden.
commonError: Student describes the character and the setting separately without explaining the connection between them.

name: Recognises recurring character-setting patterns across texts
description: Student can identify that certain types of characters appear in certain types of settings across different literary texts and explain why this pattern exists.
exampleOfSuccess: Student explains: In lots of fairytales royalty live in castles and children go into forests. Authors use these settings because castles feel powerful and safe and forests feel unknown and dangerous — they match the characters.
commonError: Student identifies the pattern by listing examples but cannot explain why those character-setting combinations recur across texts.

name: Compares how different authors connect characters to settings
description: Student can compare how two authors from different cultural contexts use setting to reflect or shape their characters, including texts by First Nations Australian authors.
exampleOfSuccess: Student compares a fairytale set in a European castle with a First Nations Australian story set on Country and explains: In the fairytale the castle shows the character has power. In the First Nations story the Country is connected to who the character is — it is part of their identity not just where they live.
commonError: Student notes that settings are different across texts but does not connect the setting to what it reveals or communicates about the characters.

name: Uses character-setting connection in own creative writing
description: Student can deliberately connect a character to a setting in their own creative writing so that the setting reflects or reveals something about the character.
exampleOfSuccess: Student writes a character who is shy and quiet and places them in a small hidden garden rather than a busy street, explaining: I chose the hidden garden because my character likes to be alone — the setting shows that without me having to say it.
commonError: Student creates a character and a setting but selects the setting randomly rather than using it to reflect or reveal the character.

name: Identifies features of a literary text
description: Student can name and describe at least two features of a literary text such as the main character, the setting, the problem and the resolution.
exampleOfSuccess: After reading a picture book, student identifies: The main character is a fox who wants to find a home. The setting is a cold forest in winter. The problem is that the fox keeps getting turned away.
commonError: Student retells the story without naming the literary features, or names a feature but cannot describe it accurately.

name: Gives a reason for a preference connected to a text feature
description: Student can state a personal preference about a literary text and connect that preference to a specific feature of the text rather than a general feeling.
exampleOfSuccess: Student says: I preferred this story to the last one because I liked the setting better — it was set on a farm and I have been to a farm so I could imagine it really clearly.
commonError: Student states a preference without connecting it to a specific feature of the text, or gives a reason that is not connected to the text at all.

name: Responds to the behaviour of non-human characters
description: Student can discuss the positive and negative behaviours of non-human characters such as animals and explain how those behaviours made them feel as a reader.
exampleOfSuccess: Student says: The fox kept lying to get what he wanted and that made me feel annoyed at him even though I wanted him to find a home. It made the story interesting because I wasn't sure if I should cheer for him.
commonError: Student describes what the character did without reflecting on how the behaviour affected them as a reader or what it made them think about the character.

name: Connects a text to own experience to explain a preference
description: Student can explain a preference for a text by making a specific connection between the text and their own experience or knowledge.
exampleOfSuccess: Student explains: I preferred stories set in familiar places because when the character went to the beach I already knew what sand feels like and what the waves sound like — it made the story feel real to me in a way a story set in space doesn't.
commonError: Student mentions a personal connection but does not use it to explain why the connection influenced their preference for that text.

name: Identifies language used to describe a character
description: Student can locate words and phrases in a literary text that describe a character and explain what impression those words create.
exampleOfSuccess: Student finds: 'the wolf grinned a wide and wicked grin' and explains: Wicked makes the wolf sound evil and the word grinned sounds sneaky — it makes you think he is up to something bad.
commonError: Student locates descriptive words but cannot explain what impression they create for the reader.

name: Identifies verb groups used to convey action and emotion
description: Student can locate verb groups in a literary text that convey how a character moves, speaks or feels and explain what those verb groups communicate beyond a simple action.
exampleOfSuccess: Student identifies 'she crept silently' and explains: Crept tells you she was moving slowly and carefully — it is more specific than walked and tells you something about how she was feeling too, like she was nervous or trying to hide.
commonError: Student identifies the verb but reads it only as a physical action without considering what it conveys about the character's emotion or motivation.

name: Compares how two authors describe the same type of character or setting
description: Student can compare the language used by two different authors to describe a similar character type or setting and identify key differences in the impression each creates.
exampleOfSuccess: Student compares two descriptions of a forest: Author A uses dark and twisted branches — Author B uses dappled sunlight through tall trees. Student explains: Both are forests but Author A makes it feel dangerous and Author B makes it feel peaceful. The language choice changes how you feel about the place.
commonError: Student notes that the descriptions are different without explaining how the language choices create different impressions for the reader.

name: Uses precise language to describe a character or setting in own writing
description: Student can deliberately select words and verb groups in their own creative writing to create a specific impression of a character or setting.
exampleOfSuccess: Student revises 'The man walked into the room' to 'The tall stranger strode into the dimly lit room' and explains: Strode makes him sound confident and powerful. Dimly lit makes the room feel mysterious.
commonError: Student adds adjectives but selects them randomly rather than deliberately choosing words that create a specific impression.

name: Identifies rhyme in a poem or song
description: Student can identify rhyming words in a poem or song and locate the pattern of rhyme within the text.
exampleOfSuccess: Student listens to a poem and identifies the rhyming pairs at the end of lines: cat/hat, moon/soon, day/play and can describe where the rhymes occur — at the end of every second line.
commonError: Student identifies that a text rhymes but cannot locate the specific rhyming words or describe the pattern.

name: Identifies and claps the rhythm of a poem or chant
description: Student can identify the rhythm of a poem or chant by clapping or tapping along and recognise whether the rhythm is regular or irregular.
exampleOfSuccess: Student claps along to a chant and identifies: Every line has the same beat — da-DUM-da-da-DUM — it is the same pattern all the way through.
commonError: Student claps along but at an inconsistent pace, not tracking the underlying rhythmic pattern.

name: Reproduces a sound or word pattern from a poem
description: Student can orally reproduce a rhythmic or rhyming pattern from a poem, chant or song, maintaining the rhythm and rhyme scheme of the original.
exampleOfSuccess: Student recites a familiar poem accurately, maintaining the correct rhythm and rhyme and not substituting words that would break the pattern.
commonError: Student reproduces the general meaning of the poem but loses the rhythm or substitutes words that break the rhyme scheme.

name: Creates new lines using a borrowed rhythmic or rhyming pattern
description: Student can compose new lines of poetry or a chant that follow the same rhythmic or rhyming pattern as a model text.
exampleOfSuccess: Given the pattern 'The __ is __ and __' from a model poem, student generates: The ocean is wild and deep. The mountain is tall and cold. — maintaining the pattern.
commonError: Student creates new content but does not maintain the rhythm or rhyme pattern of the model, producing lines that break the established pattern.

name: Experiments with sound devices in own poetry
description: Student can deliberately use rhyme, rhythm, alliteration or onomatopoeia in their own poetry and explain the effect they were aiming for.
exampleOfSuccess: Student writes a short poem using alliteration: Seven silver stars slid slowly across the sky and explains: I used lots of s sounds because it sounds smooth and quiet like stars moving.
commonError: Student includes a sound device but cannot explain why they chose it or what effect it creates for the reader.

name: Identifies structural features of a familiar literary text to adapt
description: Student can identify the key structural features of a familiar text — characters, setting, problem, resolution — that could be changed to create an adapted version.
exampleOfSuccess: Student says: In the original story the characters are three pigs and a wolf. The problem is the wolf wants to eat them. I could change the characters to three bears and a fox and have a different problem.
commonError: Student wants to retell the original story rather than identify which elements could be changed to create an adaptation.

name: Invents alternative speech or dialogue for a character
description: Student can write or perform speech or dialogue for a familiar character that fits their personality but reflects a new event or alternative outcome.
exampleOfSuccess: Given the three little pigs story, student invents dialogue for the wolf in an alternative ending where he apologises: I am sorry I scared you all. I was just cold and hungry. Could I please come in?
commonError: Student writes dialogue that does not fit the character's established personality or that simply repeats dialogue from the original text.

name: Adapts a familiar text by changing a key element
description: Student can create an adapted version of a familiar literary text by deliberately changing one key element — character, setting or problem — while maintaining the overall structure.
exampleOfSuccess: Student adapts a fairytale by changing the setting from a forest to an underwater world, adjusting details throughout so the new setting is consistent: The mermaid swam through the dark kelp forest instead of walking through the dark woods.
commonError: Student changes a surface detail such as a character's name without making consistent changes to the rest of the text to reflect the adaptation.

name: Improves descriptions by adding prepositional phrases
description: Student can add a prepositional phrase to a simple description in their own writing to make it more specific and vivid.
exampleOfSuccess: Student revises 'The dog sat.' to 'The dog sat on the old wooden step, beside the front door.' and explains: The phrases tell the reader exactly where the dog is — it creates a clearer picture.
commonError: Student adds adjectives rather than prepositional phrases, not understanding that a prepositional phrase locates or elaborates on the noun rather than simply describing it.

name: Creates and edits an adapted literary text
description: Student can write a complete adapted literary text, using familiar structures and language features from a model text, and edit it to improve descriptions and ensure consistency.
exampleOfSuccess: Student produces an adapted version of a familiar story with a new setting, consistent character voices and at least two improved descriptions using specific vocabulary or prepositional phrases added during editing.
commonError: Student produces a first draft adaptation but does not edit, leaving inconsistencies in setting or character voice and relying on vague vocabulary throughout.
